prize_parts.citation: for the development of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a discovery-plus-invention case of the kind the prize was designed for. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes first-order light shifts, so many atoms can be held in a lattice without Doppler or recoil broadening, and Ye's group turned that into the best-performing strontium clocks and into clock-comparison and many-body clock physics. Four colleagues ranked it first and two more placed it in their top three, which suggests that a broad base of the committee can support it, but my case rests on the science: independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) agree at the 10^-18 level, the concept is original, and the consequences are concrete in tests of constants and dark-sector physics, relativistic geodesy and the road to a redefinition of the second. The 2005 prize covered the frequency comb and the 1989 prize covered the separated-field and trapped-ion clock methods; the lattice clock is a distinct step that depends on detailed control of atomic structure, polarisabilities and blackbody shifts, and that is a point on which I can judge the physics directly. The two-name attribution is clean, which is rarer than it looks among this shortlist.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that atomic clocks already have two prizes behind them, and the committee may read Ye's frequency-comb heritage at JILA and Hall's 2005 recognition as making this a continuation. A second concern is that the credited pair omits others (Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde, Takamoto, and ion-clock work by Wineland and Rosenband) so the fairness of exactly two names cannot be tested from this list alone. Finally, the redefinition of the second is not yet done, and some may prefer to wait for it. I do not think any of these defeats the case, but I do think the second point deserves a frank discussion rather than being treated as settled by the count of first places.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked the lattice clock first, considers the overlap with the 2005 and 1989 prizes a presentational matter and not a bar, and ranked optical-lattice quantum simulation second, choosing Zoller with Bloch and Greiner to balance theory and experiment.
responses.response: I agree on the clock and on the 2005 overlap: the comb gave the means to count optical cycles, whereas the lattice clock is about engineering the atomic environment so that the transition is protected. On B042 I disagree about adding Zoller. His proposals with Jaksch and Cirac are decisive for the idea, but five names compete for three seats, and the three-experimentalist reading I used in my own ballot has the advantage that Mott insulators, microscopy and fermionic Hubbard physics are demonstrations rather than proposals. I accept that this leaves out Cirac and Zoller, and that is exactly why I would not make B042 my first choice this year.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked twisted bilayer graphene first because it is a specific prediction followed by a specific experiment, with broad impact, and he regards the Higgs experiments as arguably overdue.
responses.response: The prediction-then-experiment structure of B017 is real and attractive, and I ranked it seventh mainly on maturity, not on importance. The pairing mechanism in the superconducting phase is still being argued about, and Cao, the first author of the decisive experiments, is outside the credited names, so the three-name set leaves a visible gap. I disagree that this makes it ahead of the clocks today, but I would put it on my alternative list and I could be moved if colleagues show that the correlated-insulator physics is settled enough. On B002 I agree that the physics is beyond doubt; my hesitation is the one you also name, namely that honouring spokespeople and project leaders for a thousand-author discovery needs a clear justification in the citation.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED first as the architecture behind essentially all superconducting processors, and noted that the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum circuits makes the follow-up coherent and timely.
responses.response: I have a lot of sympathy for the cavity-QED analogy and I know the atomic version well, but I read the 2025 prize the other way: it recognised superconducting circuits as quantum systems, and I would expect the committee to want some distance before returning to the same hardware family. I ranked B003 sixth for that reason. I also remain unconvinced that choosing between Blais and Girvin can be done with confidence; you describe it as contestable, and I think it is more than that. If the committee prefers a quantum-technology prize, I would rather see it justified on that credit question than on the recency of the 2025 award.

responses.point: Kroll also ranked the lattice clock first and raised the question whether the committee views the 2005 comb prize as already covering the area, and he put atom interferometry second as a measurement-science candidate.
responses.response: I share the concern about overlap and have tried to answer it above: a comb prize and a lattice-clock prize recognise different problems. Atom interferometry is not on this shortlist, so I cannot argue for it here, but your concern that it would read as a technique prize rather than a discovery is one I would apply with less force to the clocks, because the clocks have already produced a specific measurement result at 10^-18 and a clear road to the redefinition of the second. I would ask you whether you see the relative weight of Katori and Ye as an obstacle to the two-name citation.

responses.point: Pearce ranked IceCube first as detector-led discovery of a new observational window, with Halzen as a single credited name, and ranked the lattice clock second.
responses.response: I agree that the detector-led case is real and that the diffuse flux is firmly established. My reservation is the same one you state: a single credited name for a collaboration of this size will draw attribution objections, and the source identifications (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) are at moderate significance, so the discovery story is still being written. This is outside my specialty and I would defer to colleagues closer to astroparticle physics on whether the early proposers and builders could be credited without leaving the shortlist.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the 2005 and 1989 prizes as already covering atomic clocks, or accept the lattice clock as a distinct step.
Whether two names are a fair allocation given that Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde, Takamoto and ion-clock contributors are outside the credited list.
Whether to wait for the formal redefinition of the second before recognising the clocks.
My judgement on B002, B017 and B003 outside atomic physics relies on general knowledge.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B001 or for my alternatives from the provided profile: none of Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer, Della Negra, Jenni or Virdee appears among my documented collaborators. I work in atomic theory and have documented collaborations with Anne L'Huillier, Ursula Keller's group, Reinhold Schuch and others; none is a credited name here, but my field proximity to the atomic-physics candidates (B001, B032, B042) should be kept in view and discounted accordingly.
